newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Namibia's Nujoma slams opposition to hydro project.
newsitem.headline: Namibia's Nujoma slams opposition to hydro project.

text.p: Namibian President Sam Nujoma said on Monday his government would not bow to opposition at home over the planned Epupa hydro-electric scheme in the north of the arid southern African country.

"The government will not be deterred by the misguided activities of those who want to impede economic development and upliftment of the standards of living of our people," he told diplomats at the opening of a heads of mission conference.

Outlining the efforts by the Ministry of Mines and Energy to increase Namibia's power supply capacity, he said the findings of the pre-feasibility study on the controversial Epupa project indicated the project was technically and financially viable.

"We fought for human rights, democracy and social change," said Nujoma, president since independence in 1990. "We refuse to succumb to sinister manipulations and misinformation of people who do not have Namibia's interest at heart."
A 23 million Namibian dollar ($4.9 million) in-depth feasibility study on the project is due for release in October.

The nomadic Himba who live in the area have opposed the planned project near the Epupa Falls on the Kunene River since it was mooted in 1991, saying it would deprive them of much-needed emergency grazing for their 60,000-odd head of cattle, and flood their ancestral graves.

Environmentalists have also voiced concern that it would destroy the flood plains of the upper Kunene and a pristine natural habitat of a multitude of fauna and flora sustaining the Himba and other people living in the area.

Namibia, a nation of 1.5 million people, draws most of its electricity from South Africa, with the Ruacana hydro-electric scheme and the coal-fired van Eck power station in Windhoek used as supplementary power sources.

The national power utility Nampower has hailed the Epupa project as clean and renewable, and the cheapest future power option. Costs for the scheme are estimated at US$480 million, but a donor has not yet been identified.
